entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gijsbrecht van Brederode (died August 24, 1475) was a prominent Dutch nobleman from the powerful House of Brederode, whose brief but tumultuous tenure as Bishop-elect of Utrecht from April 7, 1455, to August 6, 1456, ignited a significant regional conflict known as the Utrecht Schism. His election by the cathedral chapter represented a reassertion of local autonomy against the encroaching influence of the Burgundian dukes, specifically Philip the Good, who sought to install his illegitimate son, David of Burgundy, into the influential episcopal see. This clash between local ecclesiastical prerogative and burgeoning dynastic power made Gijsbrecht a pivotal, albeit short-lived, figure in the struggle for control over the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht.

Following the death of Bishop Rudolf van Diepholt, the cathedral chapter of Utrecht, exercising its traditional right, elected Gijsbrecht van Brederode as the new Prince-Bishop. This move was a direct defiance of Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, who had already secured papal provision for his son, David of Burgundy, to the same office. The ensuing power struggle saw Gijsbrecht initially supported by elements within the city and surrounding lordships, leading to a period of armed conflict. However, facing overwhelming Burgundian military and political pressure, Gijsbrecht was ultimately compelled to resign his claim to the bishopric in exchange for a substantial financial settlement of 40,000 gold guilders and a lifelong pension, along with several lordships, including Vianen and Ameide. This agreement, mediated at the Congress of Geraardsbergen in August 1456, effectively ended his direct rule but did not immediately quell the broader resistance to Burgundian authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gijsbrecht van Brederode's brief tenure and forced resignation as Bishop-elect of Utrecht marked a critical regional turning point, solidifying Burgundian power in the Low Countries and diminishing local autonomy. His story illustrates the broader struggle between dynastic expansion and traditional ecclesiastical rights in 15th-century Europe.
